semantic_correction.stem: Parents report that their toilet-trained 3-year-old has begun having occasional accidents and asking to use a bottle since a new sibling came home. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Explain that brief regression can occur during adjustment; respond without shaming, preserve one-on-one attention, and invite age-appropriate involvement with the baby.
options.B: Set firm consequences for accidents and bottle requests, reduce one-on-one attention, and praise behavior only when it matches the child's previous developmental level.
options.C: Increase focus on newborn routines and encourage the older child to manage more tasks independently, using less parental attention to speed adaptation.
options.D: Begin other planned routine changes, such as a bed transition or new child care, so the child experiences the family's changes within one adjustment period.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. The American Academy of Pediatrics' HealthyChildren guidance, updated February 10, 2026, states that preschoolers ages 2 to 4 may temporarily regress after a new baby arrives; examples specifically include new toileting accidents and wanting a bottle. The AAP advises giving the child the attention they need rather than telling the child to act their age, setting aside special one-on-one time, and inviting the older child to help in age-appropriate ways so the child feels included. The same guidance advises avoiding unnecessary major routine changes around the baby's arrival because multiple simultaneous changes can overwhelm a preschooler. B is incorrect because shaming or withdrawing needed attention conflicts with the AAP approach. C is incorrect because reducing attention and emphasizing independence can intensify the child's competition for parental attention rather than support adjustment. D is incorrect because adding major routine changes during the transition is specifically discouraged when they can be timed separately. If toileting regression becomes persistent or is accompanied by symptoms suggesting a physical problem, clinical evaluation is appropriate; the stem instead presents the exact new-sibling regression pattern described by the AAP.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Support preschool sibling adjustment to a new baby by recognizing temporary regression, maintaining reassuring one-on-one attention, encouraging age-appropriate inclusion, and avoiding unnecessary simultaneous routine changes.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests evidence-supported sibling-adjustment counseling with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current AAP guidance, and no absolute-word or answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It directly applies the AAP recommendations to normalize temporary regression, avoid shaming, provide one-on-one attention, and include the preschooler in age-appropriate ways.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Punitive consequences, reduced attention, and conditional approval conflict with the AAP recommendation to provide needed attention rather than demand age-appropriate behavior during regression.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. The AAP advises preserving special attention and inclusion; deliberately reducing parental attention is not a recommended adaptation strategy.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. The AAP specifically recommends timing major routine changes so they are not stacked on top of the new-sibling transition when avoidable.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A is the only option that combines the AAP-supported response to regression with one-on-one attention and inclusion; B is punitive, C reduces needed attention, and D adds simultaneous transitions.
cueing_check: All four choices are parallel parent-counseling strategies of comparable length and specificity; the prior 'all' distractor and uniquely-long correct answer were removed.
